title: Sanjeev Kapoor Shares Sugar-Free Multigrain Crackers Recipe Using Ragi, Jowar, and Bajra
excerpt: The Padma Shri-awarded chef's air-fried cracker recipe uses three traditional Indian millets and zero sugar, offering a healthy alternative to packaged snacks.
body:
• Chef Sanjeev Kapoor has shared a recipe for sugar-free multigrain crackers made with ragi, jowar, and bajra flours — three of India's most nutritious millets.
  • The crackers are air-fried at 180°C for about 10 minutes and require no sugar, preservatives, or refined flour.
  • Total preparation and cooking time is roughly 40 minutes, making the recipe practical for busy households.
  • Millets are naturally gluten-free, high in fiber, and rich in calcium, iron, and magnesium, according to USDA and FSSAI data.

Celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor has shared a recipe for homemade multigrain crackers that skips sugar entirely, using a trio of millet flours and an air fryer for a snack that is both crisp and nutritious.

The recipe combines finger millet (ragi), sorghum (jowar), and pearl millet (bajra) — three grains that have been staples in Indian kitchens for centuries but have gained renewed attention for their health benefits. Together, they deliver a dense nutritional profile: fiber, plant-based protein, calcium, iron, and sustained energy without the blood sugar spikes associated with refined flour snacks.

The Recipe

Kapoor's method is straightforward. Mix equal parts ragi, jowar, and bajra flour in a bowl. Add salt, carom seeds (ajwain), and crushed black pepper for flavour, then work in a spoonful of ghee for richness. Knead the mixture with water into a firm dough and let it rest under a moist cloth for 10 to 15 minutes.

Roll the dough thin between two sheets of parchment paper, sprinkle sesame seeds on top for extra crunch, and cut into squares or rectangles. Preheat the air fryer to 180°C, lightly spray the basket with olive oil, and cook the crackers for around 10 minutes until golden and crisp. Let them cool to room temperature before serving.

Total prep time runs about 25 minutes, with another 15 minutes for cooking — quick enough for a weekday afternoon, according to the recipe shared by Kapoor.

Why Millets Matter

The choice of grains is deliberate. Each of the three millets brings something different to the table. Ragi is one of the richest plant sources of calcium, with 300 to 350 milligrams per 100 grams according to data from the Indian Council of Agricultural Research — higher than any other cereal grain. Bajra leads in iron content at roughly 8 milligrams per 100 grams, making it useful for addressing anaemia. Jowar contributes 6 to 7 grams of dietary fiber per 100 grams, along with magnesium, potassium, and antioxidants.

All three are naturally gluten-free, which makes them suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity. Their low glycemic index also means they release energy gradually, helping to manage blood sugar — a relevant consideration in a country where an estimated 77 million people live with diabetes.

"Different millet varieties show strikingly distinct 'lipid fingerprints.' Some stood out for their superior nutritional profiles — particularly foxtail, finger and little millet for supporting heart health and blood glucose regulation."

— Siddabasave Gowda, Hokkaido University, published in Food Chemistry

A Shift Away From Ultra-Processed Snacking

Kapoor's recipe arrives at a time when awareness of ultra-processed foods is growing in India. Packaged crackers and biscuits — staples in many Indian households — typically contain refined flour (maida), added sugar, palm oil, and preservatives. By contrast, these homemade crackers use whole grain flours, ghee, and no sugar at all.

The crackers pair well with chutneys, hummus, or soups, and can be packed into school lunchboxes or served at tea time. They store well at room temperature in an airtight container, making them a practical make-ahead snack.

Kapoor's Continuing Influence

Kapoor, who was honoured with the Padma Shri in 2017, has long been one of India's most recognised culinary voices. His television show Khana Khazana ran for over two decades and helped shape home cooking habits across the country. In recent years, he has increasingly focused on health-conscious recipes that use traditional Indian ingredients — a shift that mirrors broader dietary trends among urban Indian consumers and the diaspora.

For Indian American Kitchens

For diaspora families, the recipe is appealing on multiple levels. Ragi, jowar, and bajra flours are now widely available at Indian grocery stores in the US and through online retailers. The air fryer method suits the appliance-heavy American kitchen, and the absence of refined sugar fits the health-first approach many Indian American parents are taking with their children's snacks.

India's push to promote millets — which gained global visibility during the UN-declared International Year of Millets in 2023 — has also made these grains more accessible and better understood outside the subcontinent.
